<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, NETworkManager is a comprehensive, full-featured open source desktop application built with .NET and WPF. Its purpose is to serve as a unified tool for network management and troubleshooting. This includes remote connections via protocols like Remote Desktop, SSH/Telnet (via PuTTY), PowerShell (WinRM), VNC (TigerVNC), as well as network analysis modules (WiFi Analyzer, IP Scanner, Port Scanner, Ping Monitor, Traceroute, DNS Lookup, LLDP/CDP Capture, etc.). There is also a dedicated website (built with Docusaurus) for documentation, downloads, and blogs and several supporting scripts for installation (Chocolatey, WinGet, etc.).

Below are the detailed steps and guidelines to create an accurate system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • User Interface (Presentation Layer): Represented by the WPF application in the “Source/NETworkManager” directory that contains Views, XAML, and controls. Also include the custom controls in “Source/NETworkManager.Controls” and the resource (styles, templates) folders.
   • MVVM Layer: The “ViewModels” folder components that act as the mediator between the UI and business logic. They implement the Model-View-ViewModel pattern and coordinate with Models.
   • Business Logic & Domain Models: All the core functionality is implemented in separate libraries such as “NETworkManager.Models”, “NETworkManager.Profiles”, “NETworkManager.Settings”, “NETworkManager.Converters”, “NETworkManager.Validators”, etc. These are responsible for managing network data, configuration, profiles (encrypted sets of hosts/networks), and interaction with external devices and protocols.
   • Utility & Infrastructure: Modules in “NETworkManager.Utilities” provide helper methods (for file operations, encryption, IP handling, etc.) and “NETworkManager.Update”, “NETworkManager.Setup” handle update distribution and installation.
   • External Integrations & Services: Identify integrations with remote system connections (Remote Desktop, PuTTY, PowerShell, TigerVNC, AWS Session Manager) and the network analysis functions (IPScanner, Ping Monitor, port scanning, traceroute, DNS lookup, SNMP, etc.). Also include external API interactions (e.g., ip-api.com for geo-IP lookups and GitHub for update checks).
   • Website & Documentation: The “Website” directory is a separate component using Docusaurus. It hosts documentation, changelogs, and releases. This can be represented as an independent subsystem that interfaces with the overall project for user documentation and web-based downloads.
   • Build & CI/CD Infrastructure: Although not part of runtime, include your continuous integration (AppVeyor workflows, GitHub Actions, dependency management files, scripts for Chocolatey, WinGet, etc.) to illustrate deployment and packaging aspects.

2. Define the Relationships and Data Flow:
   • Show how the UI (views) connects to the ViewModels — use directional arrows from UI components to view models.
   • Indicate that ViewModels invoke functionality from the Models (which encapsulate the business logic for network operations, profiles, and settings).
   • Illustrate that Models and Utility components provide the methods for network scanning, remote connections, and data conversion/validation.
   • Diagram the external service connections (for remote protocols, API calls for geolocation or updates, etc.) that are consumed in the network modules.
   • Represent the installer and updater mechanisms (derived from Setup and Update projects) which pull artifacts from build scripts and CI workflows, and then (via package managers) distribute the signed binaries.
   • Show the website component as a separate block that is linked to the project repository through documentation and release cycles.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Emphasize the use of the MVVM pattern that separates Views, ViewModels, and Models.
   • Note the modular structure where each major feature (e.g., remote connection, network scanning, settings management) is encapsulated in its own assembly or namespace.
   • Illustrate dependency injection or service location if applicable (common in large WPF projects) among the various modules.
   • The project is organized into multiple assemblies to separate concerns (UI, utilities, core business logic, external integrations, validators, etc.), so the diagram should reflect these boundaries.

4. Include Relevant Technologies and Frameworks:
   • .NET 8.x and WPF as the primary development framework for the desktop application.
   • Use of XAML for UI design, and tools like Visual Studio or Rider for development.
   • Integration of third-party libraries/frameworks like Dragablz (for tearable tabs), log4net (logging), MahApps.Metro (UI toolkit), and various converters/validators.
   • External packages (Chocolatey, WinGet) and build/CI tools (AppVeyor, GitHub Actions) which support the packaging and distribution.

5. Tailor the Diagram for a Full-Stack Desktop Application:
   • For NETworkManager, your diagram should clearly separate the desktop application (client-side) that handles all the network management aspects from supporting infrastructure (build, packaging, website/documentation).
   • Stress the separation between the “UI layer” (WPF views and controls), the “Application logic layer” (ViewModels and Models), and “Integration/Services layers” (network modules and external connections).

6. Recommended Elements and Styling for the Diagram:
   • Use clear, well-labeled boxes for each component (e.g., “WPF UI”, “View Models”, “Network Models”, “Utilities”, “External Services”, “Update/Installer Service”, “Documentation Website”).
   • Connect the components with directional arrows to indicate data flow and dependencies (e.g., UI → ViewModels, ViewModels → Models, Models → External Network Services).
   • Consider color coding or using different shapes to differentiate layers (such as rounded rectangles for UI components, standard rectangles for business logic components, and cylinders/icons for external/third-party services).
   • Include annotations for major design patterns (like MVVM) and note any significant workflows (example: user initiates a network scan from the UI, the corresponding view model triggers a method in the network model, which then uses utilities and external API calls).

7. Practical Steps to Create the Diagram:
   • Start with a high-level layout showing the three main layers: Presentation (UI), Business Logic (MVVM and Domain Models), and Infrastructure/External Services.
   • Drill down within each layer: for instance, show that the Presentation layer includes various dialogs, controls, and resource/style files, while the Business Logic layer contains sub-modules for network scanning, remote connectivity, settings and profiles.
   • Add a separate section for the ancillary components (documentation/website, CI/CD, packaging artifacts).
   • Ensure that every significant assembly or project folder (as evident from the file tree) has its corresponding component on the diagram, especially those that influence how the system runs (e.g., Setup, Update, Validators, Converters).
   • Keep the diagram detailed but logically partitioned to avoid clutter; you may use nested diagrams or layers to represent finer details.

By following these guidelines, you will create a comprehensive and detailed system design diagram that reflects the distinct parts of NETworkManager, their interactions, and the technologies involved. The diagram should capture the significant architectural elements and design principles, making it easier for the engineering team to understand, maintain, and further develop the project.
</explanation>
